title: Secret Trusts
subtitle: The unwritten promise a will was never meant to reveal
objectives: Explain why a secret trust can be enforced despite apparently failing to comply with the Wills Act 1837, s 9
State and apply the requirements for a fully secret trust, including the rule on when communication and acceptance may occur
Distinguish a half-secret trust from a fully secret trust, and identify the stricter timing rule that governs communication of a half-secret trust's terms
Describe, and hold in tension, the two competing theoretical justifications for secret trusts — the fraud theory and the 'dehors the will' theory — and recognise that neither is uncontested

leadingAuthorities.role: Sets out the modern three-element test for a fully secret trust: intention, communication, acceptance
Confirms half-secret trusts are enforceable, and that communication of the terms must occur before or at the execution of the will
A half-secret trust fails where the will's own wording is inconsistent with the timing or manner of the communication actually given
Sets the formalities (writing, signature, attestation by two witnesses) that a valid will must satisfy — the backdrop the secret trust doctrine appears to sidestep

whyThisMattersTemplate.default: Secret trusts sit in an odd corner of the syllabus — equity enforcing a promise that was, by design, kept off the face of a formally executed will. Where the profile shows application is ahead of understanding, this note appears: 'You can already apply the communication and acceptance rules — this lesson asks you to sit with why the doctrine exists at all, since the theoretical justification is genuinely contested, not settled.'

profileHooks.weakApplication: The rules here reward precision on timing — read Parts 2 and 3 slowly, since fully secret and half-secret trusts are governed by different communication deadlines, and that's where most marks are lost.
profileHooks.weakKnowledge: Start with Part 1's framing question before the case detail arrives — understanding why this doctrine needs a justification at all will make the rest of the lesson make sense, rather than feel like an arbitrary list of exceptions.

overview.hook: A woman leaves her entire estate, in a perfectly valid will, 'to my friend Harold absolutely.' Nothing in the document hints that years earlier, in a quiet conversation Harold never wrote down and nobody else witnessed, she asked him to pass most of it on to her estranged daughter after his own death — and he agreed. The will says Harold owns everything outright. Equity may say otherwise. This lesson is about a trust that exists nowhere on paper, resting on nothing but a promise made in private — and about why the law lets that promise bind a man's conscience decades later.

parts.heading: A promise the will was never meant to show
parts.voice: Socratic and atmospheric — sits with the puzzle before offering any resolution
body: Here is the puzzle this whole lesson circles, and it's worth feeling its full strangeness before you learn how equity resolves it. Parliament decided, in the Wills Act 1837, that a testamentary gift is only valid if it is written down, signed by the testator, and witnessed by two people signing in the testator's presence. The formalities exist for good reason: they guard against fraud, against undue pressure on the dying, against disputes about what a dead person 'really' wanted that can never be resolved because the only witness who could resolve them is gone.

A secret trust asks you to accept something that looks, on its face, like exactly the danger those formalities were built to prevent: a testator's true wishes, recorded nowhere in the will itself, proved only by the oral testimony of the very person who stands to gain — or in a half-secret trust's case, who at least controls — the property. And yet English equity enforces these arrangements. It has done so for over three hundred years. Why would it undermine, in this one context, the exact protection Parliament went to such trouble to build?

Hold that question loosely as you read on, because there isn't a single, agreed answer — this is one of the few doctrines on the syllabus where the leading theoretical explanations genuinely compete, and examiners reward students who can hold both in view rather than picking one and pretending the debate is settled. What's certain is the practical shape of the doctrine; what's contested is why it exists at all. We'll take the shape first, and the theory last, in Part 5 — deliberately, so the theory has real cases to be a theory about.

components.definition: A trust of property passing under a will (or on intestacy) whose existence, or whose precise terms, are not disclosed on the face of the will itself, but which equity will enforce against the person who received the property, on proof that they agreed during the testator's lifetime to hold it for someone else.

interaction.prompt: A will leaves a house 'to my brother absolutely,' with nothing more said anywhere in the document. If the brother in fact promised the testator, in a private conversation years before, to hold the house for the testator's goddaughter — could equity ever enforce that promise despite the will's silence?
options: Yes — this is precisely the situation the secret trust doctrine exists to address
No — anything not written into the will itself is legally irrelevant
interaction.feedbackCorrect: Correct, and this is the doctrine in its purest form: a will that looks like an outright gift, sitting alongside a private promise equity may still enforce against the person named as owner.
interaction.feedbackIncorrect: Not quite — this is exactly the scenario secret trusts address. The will's silence is the point: equity looks past the document to the private arrangement, provided the right elements (which the rest of this lesson sets out) are proved.

parts.heading: The fully secret trust: three things to prove
parts.voice: case-narrative — builds the doctrine directly out of one governing case
body: A fully secret trust is the starker version of the puzzle: the will discloses nothing at all — not even the existence of a trust. On its face, the recipient simply inherits outright. Ottaway v Norman gives the modern statement of what a claimant must prove to unseat that appearance.

Harry Ottaway told his housekeeper, Eva Hodges, that he wished to leave her his bungalow, its contents, and a sum of money, on the understanding — which she accepted — that she would leave the bungalow to his son William when she herself died. His will left the property to her outright, with no mention of William at all. After Harry died, Eva made a new will leaving the bungalow to someone else entirely. William sued to enforce the secret trust.

Brightman J held that a fully secret trust requires three things, each of which must be proved to the ordinary civil standard: (1) an **intention** by the testator that the recipient should hold the property on trust, not take it beneficially; (2) **communication** of that intention to the recipient, which may happen at any point during the testator's lifetime — before or after the will is made — provided it happens before the testator dies; and (3) **acceptance** by the recipient, which can be express or simply inferred from silent acquiescence once the terms are communicated. On the facts, William succeeded: Eva had clearly understood and accepted the arrangement, and could not defeat it by later changing her own will.

components.factsShort: A testator left his bungalow to his housekeeper outright by will, having privately obtained her agreement to leave it to his son on her own death; she later tried to leave it elsewhere instead.
components.ratioShort: A fully secret trust requires proof of intention, communication to the recipient during the testator's lifetime, and acceptance by the recipient — express or by silent acquiescence.

expanded.facts: Harry Ottaway's will left his bungalow, 'Ashcroft', its furniture, and £1,500 to his housekeeper Eva Hodges 'absolutely', with the understanding, communicated to and accepted by her before his death, that she would leave the property by her own will to Harry's son William Ottaway. Eva outlived Harry, but her own subsequent will left the bungalow to a different beneficiary, in breach of the arrangement. William claimed the bungalow was held on a secret trust for him.
expanded.judgmentExtract: Brightman J held that to establish a fully secret trust the claimant must show the testator intended the recipient to be bound (not merely to receive a moral request they were free to ignore), that this intention was communicated to the recipient, and that the recipient accepted the obligation. He further held that the same reasoning that binds a recipient to hold specific identified property on trust can, on appropriate evidence, extend to binding them not to deal with their own subsequent estate inconsistently with the arrangement — hence Eva's own later will could not override William's claim.
expanded.significance: Ottaway v Norman remains the standard modern statement of the fully secret trust test, and is also the leading authority for the point that a secret trust obligation can survive and bind what happens to the property even after it passes into the recipient's own estate, not merely during their lifetime.

components.label: Fully secret trust — the three elements (Ottaway v Norman)
points: Intention — the testator must have intended the recipient to be legally bound, not merely to receive a hoped-for request they were free to decline
Communication — the intention must be communicated to the recipient at some point during the testator's lifetime, whether before or after the will was executed
Acceptance — the recipient must accept the obligation, either expressly or by silence/acquiescence once the terms are known

interaction.prompt: In the passage below, adapted from Ottaway v Norman, highlight the sentence that states the test for a fully secret trust.
interaction.passage: The claimant relied on the housekeeper's clear understanding of the arrangement. It was established, first, that the testator must intend the recipient to take the property subject to a binding obligation and not as an absolute gift; second, that this intention must be communicated to the recipient; and third, that the recipient must accept the obligation, whether by express agreement or by acquiescence. All three elements were made out on the evidence before the court.
interaction.ratioSentence: It was established, first, that the testator must intend the recipient to take the property subject to a binding obligation and not as an absolute gift; second, that this intention must be communicated to the recipient; and third, that the recipient must accept the obligation, whether by express agreement or by acquiescence.

parts.heading: Formalities on paper, evasion in substance? The Wills Act 1837, s 9
parts.voice: analytical — reads the statute closely against the doctrine it appears to bypass
body: It's worth reading the actual formalities section, because the tension it creates with secret trusts is the whole reason this doctrine needs any theoretical justification at all. Section 9 of the Wills Act 1837 sets out what a will requires to be valid: it must be in writing and signed by the testator (or someone else in their presence, at their direction); the testator must intend by that signature to give effect to the will; and the signature must be made or acknowledged in the presence of two witnesses, who then also sign.

None of a secret trust's terms appear anywhere in this formally executed document. The recipient's name and the fact of a gift to them do appear — that part of the will is perfectly valid under s 9. What's missing from the will is the trust itself: the obligation the recipient is actually under. If a court simply asked 'does this document comply with s 9 in respect of the trust terms?', the answer would always be no, because by definition a secret trust's terms are never written into the will.

This is precisely why secret trusts cannot be explained as an ordinary application of the Wills Act — they have to be explained as sitting outside it, or despite it, on some basis equity supplies independently of testamentary formality. Keep that tension in view through the rest of this lesson: whatever the correct theory turns out to be (Part 5), it has to answer this specific question — why does a trust with no compliant documentary trace of its own terms still bind?

components.text: No will shall be valid unless it is in writing, and signed by the testator, or by some other person in his presence and by his direction; and it appears that the testator intended by his signature to give effect to the will; and the signature is made or acknowledged by the testator in the presence of two or more witnesses present at the same time; and each witness either attests and signs the will, or acknowledges his signature, in the presence of the testator.
elements: Signed by the testator (or by another, in the testator's presence and at their direction)
Testator intends the signature to give effect to the will
Signature made or acknowledged in the presence of two witnesses present together
Each witness attests and signs, or acknowledges their own signature, in the testator's presence

interaction.prompt: Which part of a secret trust arrangement is actually validated by the testator's compliance with s 9 of the Wills Act 1837?
options: Only the outright gift as it appears on the face of the will — the trust obligation itself has no separate s 9 compliance of its own
The entire arrangement, including the trust terms, because s 9 is satisfied by the will as a whole
Nothing — a will containing a secret trust is invalid under s 9 in its entirety
interaction.explanation: Section 9 formalities are satisfied for the will as executed — which, on its face, is an outright gift to the recipient. The trust obligation itself never appears in that document and so is never tested against s 9 at all; its validity has to rest on some basis independent of the statute, which is exactly the theoretical problem Part 5 addresses.

parts.heading: The trap that catches half-secret trusts: when must the terms be communicated?
parts.voice: direct — names the trap early and drills the timing distinction hard
body: A half-secret trust is a different animal from a fully secret one, and the difference matters enormously for timing. In a half-secret trust, the will itself discloses that the recipient takes as a trustee — it says so on the face of the document — but it does not say who the beneficiaries are or what the terms are. The will announces a trust and conceals only its content.

Blackwell v Blackwell confirmed that half-secret trusts are enforceable on essentially the same footing as fully secret ones — but the House of Lords also fixed a stricter timing rule for when the terms must be communicated to the trustees: communication (and their acceptance) must happen before or at the time the will is executed. This is the single most examined distinction in the whole topic, so state it precisely: fully secret trusts allow communication any time up to death; half-secret trusts require it no later than execution of the will.

Why the difference? Because a half-secret trust's own wording already tells the world a trust exists. Allowing communication of the terms after execution would let a testator effectively rewrite the beneficiaries of a will, informally, at any later date, while pointing to a document that on its face already declares a trust — a much easier route to exactly the kind of unattested, unwitnessed alteration s 9 exists to prevent. A fully secret trust carries no such visible label, so the same risk does not arise in the same way.

Re Keen shows how strictly this can bite. A testator's will empowered his trustees to hold a sum 'upon trust for such person or persons as may be notified by me to my trustees' — before execution, he had in fact given one trustee a sealed envelope naming the beneficiary, to be opened only after his death. The Court of Appeal held the trust failed: the will's own wording contemplated a future notification, but the actual communication had already happened before the will was executed, in a form (a sealed instruction, not yet opened) inconsistent with what the will described. The lesson is not just 'communicate on time' — the manner of communication must also match what the will itself says will happen.

components.commonWrongAnswer: Students very commonly apply the fully secret trust rule — 'communication any time before death' — to a half-secret trust fact pattern, especially where the will itself only says 'trustees to be informed of the beneficiaries' without specifying a date.
components.whyItsWrong: Blackwell v Blackwell sets a different, stricter deadline for half-secret trusts specifically: communication and acceptance must occur before or at the execution of the will, not merely before death. A half-secret trust communicated only after the will was signed fails outright, however clearly it was communicated and accepted afterwards — the timing defect cannot be cured by later conduct.

interaction.prompt: A will states: 'I leave £50,000 to my solicitor upon the trusts I have communicated to him.' The testator in fact tells the solicitor the beneficiary's name and share two weeks after signing the will, and the solicitor accepts. Does the half-secret trust take effect?
options: Yes — the solicitor accepted, and that is enough for any secret trust
No — communication of a half-secret trust's terms must occur before or at the execution of the will; communication two weeks afterwards is too late
Yes — because the will itself refers to trusts having been communicated, timing does not matter
interaction.trapExplanation: The first and third options both ignore Blackwell v Blackwell's specific timing rule for half-secret trusts. It is not enough that the will refers to communicated trusts, and it is not enough that the trustee later accepted — the communication itself must have happened no later than execution. Communicating two weeks after signing is fatal, regardless of how clearly the terms were later accepted.

parts.heading: Two theories, one contested puzzle
parts.voice: atmospheric and deliberately even-handed — presents the debate as live, not settled
body: Return now to the question Part 1 left open: why does equity enforce a trust with no compliant trace of its own terms on the will? Two competing explanations have been offered, and English law has never fully committed to one over the other — this is genuinely contested doctrinal territory, and treating it as settled is itself a common exam error.

The **fraud theory** is the older explanation, rooted in the original justification for enforcing secret trusts at all: it would be a fraud on the testator, and unjust enrichment of the recipient, to let someone who agreed to hold property for another then simply keep it, hiding behind the Wills Act's formalities as a shield. On this view, equity intervenes not because it respects testamentary formality, but because it refuses to let statutory formality become an instrument of fraud — the trust is enforced to stop the recipient's dishonesty, and the Wills Act is simply not allowed to protect that dishonesty.

The **dehors the will** ('outside the will') theory, associated with the reasoning increasingly favoured after Blackwell v Blackwell, explains secret trusts differently: the trust does not derive its validity from the will at all, and so is not a testamentary disposition requiring s 9 compliance in the first place. Instead, it is said to operate inter vivos — arising from the testator's lifetime declaration and the recipient's lifetime acceptance of it — with the will merely providing the mechanism by which legal title later reaches the trustee. On this view there is no real tension with the Wills Act, because the trust was never a 'will' in the relevant sense to begin with; it sits outside (dehors) the will entirely.

Neither theory is fully satisfying on its own, and examiners know it. The fraud theory struggles to explain half-secret trusts cleanly, since a half-secret trustee who simply kept the property could not claim it as their own in the first place — the will already says they take as trustee, so there is no obvious 'fraud' of the fully-secret kind for equity to prevent, yet half-secret trusts are enforced anyway. The dehors-the-will theory struggles to explain why, if the trust really is a separate inter vivos arrangement, its subject matter still has to be identifiable property passing under that specific will, and why courts still often reach for fraud-based language when justifying results on the facts. Hold both theories in mind, know which problem each one solves and which it doesn't, and resist collapsing the debate into a single 'the answer is X' — because there isn't yet a single answer the courts have committed to.

components.title: Two theories of secret trusts — what each one is built to explain
components.description: A comparison of the fraud theory and the dehors-the-will theory, and the problem each addresses.

nodes.label: Why does a trust with no s 9-compliant terms of its own still bind?
Fraud theory: equity stops the recipient using the Wills Act as a shield for dishonestly keeping property they agreed to hold for another
Dehors the will theory: the trust arises inter vivos, outside the will, so s 9 was never engaged by it in the first place
Weak spot: hard to identify a 'fraud' in half-secret trusts, where the trustee never could have claimed the property beneficially
Weak spot: hard to explain why the trust must still relate to property passing under that specific will, if it is truly a separate lifetime arrangement

components.textAlternative: The problem both theories try to solve: why does a secret trust bind when its terms are never compliant with s 9 of the Wills Act? The fraud theory answers that equity prevents the recipient from using the Wills Act as a shield for dishonestly keeping property they agreed to hold for someone else — but this struggles to explain half-secret trusts, where the trustee could never have claimed the property beneficially in the first place, so there is no obvious fraud to prevent. The dehors-the-will theory answers that the trust arises from a lifetime declaration and acceptance, operating outside the will and never engaging s 9 at all — but this struggles to explain why the trust must still relate to property passing under that specific will if it is genuinely a separate lifetime arrangement.

interaction.prompt: How confident are you that English law has settled, definitively, on a single theoretical justification for secret trusts?
sliderLabels: Genuinely unsettled — both theories remain live
interaction.explanation: This is deliberately not settled, and treating it as settled is a common exam error. Courts have used language consistent with both the fraud theory and the dehors-the-will theory at different points, and each theory has a well-recognised weak spot the other does not fully share. The honest position is that both remain live explanations, each solving a problem the other does not.

testPool.prompt: Name the three elements Ottaway v Norman requires to establish a fully secret trust.
testPool.modelAnswer: Intention that the recipient be bound, communication of that intention to the recipient during the testator's lifetime, and acceptance of the obligation by the recipient, express or by acquiescence.

testPool.prompt: In a half-secret trust, does the will disclose the existence of a trust on its face?
options: Yes — the will shows a trust exists, but conceals its terms and beneficiaries
No — nothing about a trust appears anywhere in the will

testPool.prompt: Which of the following is the correct timing rule for communicating the terms of a half-secret trust?
options: Any time before the testator's death
Before or at the time the will is executed
Within a reasonable time after the will is executed
At any time, provided the trustee later confirms acceptance in writing
testPool.trapExplanation: The first option states the fully secret trust rule, not the half-secret rule — a very common confusion. Blackwell v Blackwell requires communication of a half-secret trust's terms no later than execution of the will itself; later acceptance, however clear, cannot cure late communication.

testPool.prompt: Why can a secret trust's terms never themselves be tested for compliance with s 9 of the Wills Act 1837?
options: Because the terms, by definition, are never written into the will document that s 9 formalities apply to
Because s 9 only applies to gifts of land, not to trusts of any kind
Because secret trusts are exempted from s 9 by a specific proviso within the section
testPool.explanation: Section 9 sets formalities for the will as a document. A secret trust's terms, whether fully or half secret, are by definition kept off that document — so there is nothing for s 9 to test in respect of the trust itself, only in respect of the outright or trustee gift that does appear on the will's face.

testPool.prompt: In the passage below, adapted from Blackwell v Blackwell, highlight the sentence stating the timing rule for half-secret trusts.
testPool.passage: The appellants argued that a trust not disclosed on the face of the will could never be given effect. Their Lordships rejected that argument and held that a half-secret trust is enforceable provided its terms were communicated to, and accepted by, the trustees before or at the time the will was executed. Communication occurring only after execution cannot validate the trust, however clearly it is later accepted.
testPool.ratioSentence: Their Lordships rejected that argument and held that a half-secret trust is enforceable provided its terms were communicated to, and accepted by, the trustees before or at the time the will was executed.

testPool.prompt: Which scenario describes a fully secret trust, rather than a half-secret trust?
testPool.scenarioA: A will leaves £20,000 'to my cousin Aidan absolutely,' with no mention of any trust; Aidan had privately agreed, before the will was made, to pass most of it to a named charity.
testPool.scenarioB: A will leaves £20,000 'to my cousin Aidan, upon the trusts I have communicated to him,' without naming the beneficiaries in the will itself.
testPool.explanation: A is fully secret: the will shows nothing but an outright gift, with the trust entirely hidden. B is half-secret: the will's own wording announces that Aidan takes as trustee, even though it withholds the beneficiaries' names and shares.

testPool.prompt: A testator's will, signed on 1 March, leaves her flat 'to my niece absolutely.' On 1 May, two months later, the testator tells her niece she wants her to hold the flat for a family friend, and the niece agrees. The testator dies in June without changing her will. Is the trust enforceable?
options: Yes — this is a fully secret trust, and communication any time before death, including after the will, is sufficient
No — communication after the will was executed is always too late for any secret trust
No — because the niece must also sign the will herself to be bound
testPool.explanation: The will discloses nothing about a trust at all, so this is fully secret, not half-secret — and Ottaway v Norman allows communication and acceptance at any point during the testator's lifetime, including well after execution. The stricter before-or-at-execution rule applies only to half-secret trusts.

testPool.prompt: A will, signed on 1 March, leaves a sum 'to my accountant upon trusts already communicated to him.' The testator had in fact told the accountant the beneficiary's identity on 1 April, a month after the will was signed. Is the half-secret trust valid?
options: No — communication on 1 April is after execution on 1 March, so the trust fails despite the will's own wording suggesting communication had already occurred
Yes — because the will refers to communication having already happened, the court will treat that as satisfied
Yes — because a month's delay is short enough to be within a reasonable grace period
testPool.explanation: The actual date of communication controls, not the will's wording about it. Since the true communication happened after execution, the half-secret trust fails under Blackwell v Blackwell's timing rule — and the mismatch between what the will implies and what actually happened echoes the specific problem in Re Keen.

testPool.prompt: In Re Keen, why did the half-secret trust fail even though the beneficiary's name had genuinely been communicated to a trustee before the will was executed?
options: Because the manner of communication (a sealed envelope, to be opened after death) was inconsistent with what the will itself said would happen (future notification)
Because half-secret trusts can never be communicated by a sealed envelope under any circumstances
Because the trustee who held the envelope was not one of the will's named executors
testPool.trapExplanation: The failure was not about timing alone — communication genuinely occurred before execution. The problem was a mismatch in substance: the will's wording contemplated a notification still to come, but the actual mechanism used (an already-sealed envelope, given in advance) did not match that description. Re Keen is a trap precisely because students assume any pre-execution communication is safe.

testPool.prompt: Order the events in Ottaway v Norman.
items: Harry Ottaway tells his housekeeper Eva he wants his bungalow left to his son William after her death, and she agrees
Harry's will leaves the bungalow to Eva 'absolutely', with no mention of William
Harry dies; Eva inherits the bungalow under the will
Eva makes her own will leaving the bungalow to someone other than William

testPool.prompt: A testator's will states: 'I leave my shares in Meridian Ltd to my brother Tobias, in full confidence that he will use them as I have asked.' Before the will was signed, the testator had told Tobias privately that he wanted the shares split between two named cousins, and Tobias agreed. Analyse whether Tobias holds the shares on a secret trust for the cousins, or takes them beneficially.
factsToOrder: The will's wording ('in full confidence that he will use them as I have asked') hints at an obligation without stating a trust in terms usually associated with legal duty
Communication of the specific beneficiaries and shares occurred before the will was executed
Tobias agreed to the arrangement when it was communicated to him
The will does not, on ordinary reading, disclose to the world that a trust exists

scaffolds.support: Full model IRAC answer shown, with each fact mapped to Issue / Rule / Application / Conclusion
Rule and Issue given; student drags facts into Application and writes Conclusion
Issue given only; student selects the Rule, drags facts into Application, writes Conclusion
No scaffold; student writes full IRAC unaided

modelAnswer.issue: Whether Tobias holds the Meridian Ltd shares on a secret trust for the two cousins, and if so whether it is analysed as a fully secret or half-secret trust.
modelAnswer.rule: A fully secret trust requires intention, communication to the recipient during the testator's lifetime, and acceptance (Ottaway v Norman); it applies where the will itself does not disclose that a trust exists at all, as opposed to a half-secret trust, where the will's own wording shows a trust but withholds its terms, and which requires communication before or at execution (Blackwell v Blackwell).
modelAnswer.application: The will's language is ambiguous but, read most naturally, gifts the shares to Tobias without clearly announcing a trust to the world — 'in full confidence' is precatory-sounding rather than an explicit trust declaration, pointing towards treating this as fully secret rather than half-secret. On that basis, all three Ottaway v Norman elements are satisfied: intention (the arrangement was specific, naming beneficiaries and shares, not a vague hope), communication before the will was signed, and acceptance by Tobias. Even if a court instead read the wording as disclosing a trust and treated it as half-secret, the outcome is unaffected here because communication happened before execution, satisfying Blackwell v Blackwell's stricter deadline too.
modelAnswer.conclusion: Tobias holds the shares on trust for the two cousins; the arrangement satisfies the requirements of a secret trust whichever classification is preferred, since communication and acceptance both occurred before the will was executed.

testPool.prompt: How confident are you that the fraud theory fully explains why half-secret trusts are enforced?
testPool.explanation: The fraud theory sits more awkwardly with half-secret trusts than fully secret ones: because the will already shows the recipient takes as trustee, they could never simply keep the property as their own — so there is no obvious act of fraudulent retention for equity to be preventing, and yet half-secret trusts are enforced regardless.

testPool.prompt: Which statement best captures the 'dehors the will' theory of secret trusts?
options: The trust is a testamentary disposition and must therefore comply fully with s 9 of the Wills Act
The trust arises from a lifetime declaration and acceptance operating outside the will, so it was never a disposition requiring s 9 compliance in the first place
The trust is valid only because the recipient later ratifies it after the testator's death
testPool.trapExplanation: The first option gets the theory backwards — dehors the will exists precisely to explain why s 9 is not engaged. The third option invents a ratification requirement that plays no role in either recognised theory. The correct account treats the trust as an inter vivos arrangement that the will merely triggers the transfer of legal title for, not as a testamentary gift in its own right.

testPool.prompt: Is it accurate to say English law has fully and finally chosen between the fraud theory and the dehors-the-will theory of secret trusts?
options: No — both remain live, contested explanations, each with an acknowledged weak spot
Yes — the dehors-the-will theory has been formally adopted to the exclusion of the fraud theory
testPool.feedbackCorrect: Right, and this is worth stating plainly on an exam script rather than picking a side and presenting it as settled — the debate genuinely remains open.
testPool.feedbackIncorrect: Not settled — this is one of the few genuinely contested theoretical points on the syllabus, and treating either theory as the single, established answer overstates the current state of the law.

debriefConfig.trapSummary: The single most common mistake in this lesson's test items is applying the fully secret trust's lenient 'any time before death' communication rule to a half-secret trust fact pattern. Check first which type of trust the will's own wording describes — disclosed-trust-with-hidden-terms (half-secret) or fully silent (fully secret) — because that classification decides which timing rule governs, and the two rules are not interchangeable.
